lesson.title: The Seventeenth Amendment: Taking the Senate Out of State Legislatures' Hands
lesson.summary: Ratified in April 1913, the Seventeenth Amendment replaced the original constitutional system of state legislatures choosing U.S. senators with direct election by the voters of each state, a reform driven by widespread corruption, legislative deadlock, and muckraking exposes of senators' ties to corporate interests.
lesson.body:
The Constitution as originally written had state legislatures, not voters, choose United States senators, a design meant to give state governments a direct voice in the federal system and to insulate the Senate from the passions of popular opinion. By the late nineteenth century, this system was producing serious problems. State legislative elections for senator were vulnerable to bribery and corporate influence in ways statewide popular elections were not, since it took far less money to buy the votes of a few dozen legislators than to win over an entire state's electorate. Deadlocked legislatures, split between competing factions, sometimes left senate seats vacant for months or even years. And critics increasingly argued that senators chosen this way owed their loyalty to the corporations and party bosses who had maneuvered them into office rather than to ordinary voters.

This critique fit naturally within the broader Progressive Era argument that Gilded Age politics had let concentrated wealth capture democratic institutions, and muckraking journalism gave the case its most vivid ammunition. David Graham Phillips's 1906 magazine series The Treason of the Senate, published in Cosmopolitan, accused a long list of sitting senators of serving railroad, banking, and industrial interests rather than the public, popularizing the derisive nickname the millionaires' club for the chamber. While Phillips's specific charges were sometimes overstated, the series crystallized public suspicion that had been building for years and turned direct election of senators into a mainstream reform demand rather than a fringe position associated mainly with the earlier Populist movement, which had called for the change back in the 1890s.

Reform did not wait entirely for a constitutional amendment. A number of states developed workarounds in the early 1900s, most notably the so-called Oregon system, under which voters cast a nonbinding preference vote for senator that state legislatures then generally honored when making their official selection, effectively achieving popular election within the existing constitutional framework. These state experiments built confidence that direct election could work in practice and added pressure on Congress to make the change formal and universal.

Congress passed the amendment in 1912, and it was ratified by the states in April 1913, around the same time as the Sixteenth Amendment's ratification that February. Together the two amendments reflected the same underlying Progressive Era logic that animated debates over federalism throughout the period: that federal constitutional structures inherited from the eighteenth century needed updating to prevent concentrated economic power from subverting representative government, whether through an unfair tax system or through a legislative body insulated from the voters it was supposed to represent.
